guidance.summary: Every person, automated process (service account) and device that accesses the CUI environment must have its own unique identifier so activity can be traced back to it. In practice that means one named account per person, named service accounts for scheduled jobs and integrations, and a way to identify each device (domain computer account, certificate, or at least serial and MAC in the inventory).
guidance.machine_shop_example: Each of the 40 employees has a unique AD/Entra account such as jsmith rather than 'shopfloor1', and the CNC operators each sign into the controllers with their own account instead of a shared 'operator' login. The nightly backup and the ERP-to-CAM integration run as documented service accounts (svc-backup, svc-erpsync). All 25 PCs, the server and both controllers are domain-joined with computer accounts and appear in the RMM inventory by hostname and serial; the CUI Wi-Fi uses 802.1X with device certificates so unknown devices cannot join and are visible if they try.
typical_evidence: AD/Entra user export showing one account per person and no shared accounts (or a documented, approved exception)
Service account inventory listing each process account, the system it runs on, its purpose and owner
Device inventory (RMM, Intune or AD computer objects) with hostname, serial and MAC address
Account provisioning procedure with a naming standard and a sample onboarding ticket
Screenshot of the CNC controller login showing individual operator accounts
common_gaps: Shared 'shop' or 'operator' accounts on floor PCs and CNC controllers
Service accounts undocumented, or applications running under a person's account
Devices not tracked; personal phones and laptops on the same Wi-Fi as CUI systems with no identification
Generic admin accounts ('admin', 'msp') used by several people
remediation_steps: Export all accounts from AD/Entra and from each local system (controllers, firewall, ERP); flag shared or generic accounts and convert them to per-person accounts; if a controller cannot support individual logins, document the exception with compensating controls (sign-in log, physical access limits).
Create a service account inventory (name, system, purpose, owner, last review date) and move application processes that run under user accounts to dedicated service accounts.

Ensure every device is identified: domain- or Entra-join all PCs and controllers, keep the RMM/asset inventory current with serial and MAC, and enable 802.1X or at minimum device registration on the CUI Wi-Fi.
Write the provisioning procedure (HR notice, ticket, unique username standard, account creation) and apply it consistently for employees, contractors and MSP staff.
Review the user, service account and device lists quarterly and disable or remove anything unknown.

guidance.summary: Nothing gets into the systems without proving who or what it is: users with passwords plus MFA, service accounts with unique credentials or keys, and devices with certificates, domain membership or equivalent. It also covers managing those authenticators: changing vendor defaults, setting minimum password rules, issuing credentials securely and revoking them when no longer needed.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Users authenticate to their PCs and to GCC High with a password plus MFA; the built-in local administrator on each PC has a unique LAPS-managed password. Service accounts have unique 25+ character passwords stored in the MSP's vault and rotated annually. Both CNC controllers require a login (Windows auto-logon removed), and the default vendor passwords on the controller software, firewall, switches and printers were changed at installation and recorded in the vault. The CUI Wi-Fi uses WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise with device certificates, so only company devices can connect; guests use a separate SSID with no path to the CUI network.
typical_evidence: Authenticator management policy (minimum password length, MFA, default credential changes, secure issuance, revocation on termination)
GPO or Entra password policy screenshots and MFA/Conditional Access configuration
Vault entries or a record showing default credentials were changed on the firewall, switches, printers, ERP and CNC controller software
Wi-Fi 802.1X/RADIUS or NAC configuration showing device authentication, and the guest network separation
Service account list with credential rotation dates
Offboarding ticket showing credentials disabled and revoked
common_gaps: Vendor default passwords still in place on network gear, printers or CNC controller software
CNC controller auto-logs into Windows with no password so the machine starts faster
Guest devices and CUI devices on the same pre-shared-key Wi-Fi
Service account passwords never rotated; former MSP staff still know them
remediation_steps: Write the authenticator management policy: minimum password length (for example 14 characters), MFA wherever supported, default credential change on every new device, credentials stored only in the vault, service account rotation (annually and on staff change), and revocation on termination.

Enforce user authentication in AD/Entra: no blank or auto-logon passwords (remove AutoAdminLogon on the controllers), LAPS for local admin accounts, and account lockout after a defined number of failed attempts.
Change every default credential on the firewall, switches, access points, printers, ERP and CNC software and record them in the vault.
Authenticate devices: domain/Entra join, 802.1X with certificates (or at minimum WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise) for CUI Wi-Fi, a separate guest SSID, and certificate- or device-based VPN for remote access.
Give each service account a unique long credential, document the rotation schedule, and complete one rotation as evidence.
Add credential revocation to the offboarding checklist and verify it with a sample ticket.

guidance.summary: List which accounts are privileged (admins), then require MFA for those accounts everywhere, including logging on locally at the console, and require MFA for every user when they access systems over the network (file server, GCC High, VPN, RDP). The DoD scoring gives partial credit (3 points off instead of 5) when MFA covers remote and privileged users but not general users, but a CMMC certification assessment needs all four objectives met.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's privileged account list names the admin's Domain Admin account, two MSP engineer accounts and the Entra Global Administrator. All users sign into GCC High with Microsoft Authenticator (number matching), the VPN requires MFA, and the domain-joined PCs use Windows Hello for Business (PIN or fingerprint backed by the TPM) so every network access to the file server is MFA-backed. Admin console logins on the server and PCs use a FIDO2 security key, and the firewall admin interface requires a TOTP code. The two CNC controllers are isolated on their own VLAN, operators log in locally with non-privileged accounts, and the SSP documents that arrangement.
typical_evidence: Privileged account inventory
Entra Conditional Access policy requiring MFA for all users and all admin roles (screenshot) and the MFA registration report
Windows Hello for Business, smart card or FIDO2 configuration and the enrollment report for domain-joined PCs
VPN and firewall administrator MFA configuration screenshots
Sign-in logs showing MFA satisfied for network and privileged access
Documented exceptions (for example CNC controller local login) with compensating controls and approval
common_gaps: MFA on email only; the file server, VPN or RDP still accept a password alone
Admins log on locally at the server console with just a password
'Remember MFA for 90 days' or legacy authentication protocols left enabled, which bypass MFA
A shared operator account on the controllers with no MFA and no documented exception
remediation_steps: Identify and document the privileged accounts: Domain Admins, local Administrators, Entra admin roles, firewall/switch admins, and MSP accounts.
Enforce MFA for network access for all users: Entra Conditional Access requiring MFA for all cloud apps in GCC High, MFA on the VPN and any RDP gateway, and block legacy authentication.

Bring the domain-joined Windows logon under MFA with Windows Hello for Business (hybrid-joined, PIN/biometric backed by TPM) or FIDO2 keys/smart cards, so access to the file server and other network resources is MFA-backed.

Require MFA for privileged local access: FIDO2 or smart card for admin console logins on the server and PCs, TOTP or a hardware token for the firewall and switch admin interfaces, and MFA on the MSP's remote tools.

For CNC controllers that cannot support MFA, keep them on an isolated VLAN with non-privileged local accounts, no CUI stored beyond the current job, and document the arrangement and compensating controls in the SSP.
Review the MFA registration and sign-in reports monthly and keep them as evidence.

guidance.summary: Authentication over the network must use protocols an attacker cannot simply record and replay: Kerberos, TLS-protected logins, challenge-response, time-based one-time codes, FIDO2. Practically, that means no LM/NTLMv1, no cleartext or basic authentication, and MFA methods based on one-time codes or keys, for both privileged and non-privileged accounts.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's domain uses Kerberos for logons; LM and NTLMv1 are refused by GPO (LAN Manager authentication level set to 'Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM & NTLM'), and NTLM auditing shows only one legacy CNC share still using NTLMv2, which is documented. GCC High logins use Microsoft Authenticator with number matching over TLS, the VPN uses IKEv2 with certificates plus a TOTP code, and legacy authentication (POP/IMAP/SMTP basic) is blocked in the tenant.
typical_evidence: GPO export showing 'Network security: LAN Manager authentication level' set to NTLMv2 only / refuse LM & NTLM
Entra Conditional Access or Exchange authentication policy showing legacy authentication blocked
MFA method configuration (Authenticator with number matching, TOTP, FIDO2)
VPN configuration showing IKEv2/TLS with MFA
SSP or policy statement listing approved authentication protocols
common_gaps: NTLMv1 or LM still enabled for old CNC controllers or printers
Basic authentication left enabled for scanner-to-email or old mail clients
Internal web applications or device admin pages that log in over plain HTTP
SMS as the only MFA factor, which is weak even though it is technically replay-resistant
remediation_steps: Set the LAN Manager authentication level to 5 (send NTLMv2 only, refuse LM & NTLM) by GPO, enable NTLM auditing, and remediate any device that still needs NTLMv1.
Block legacy authentication in the GCC High tenant (Conditional Access block and Exchange authentication policies).
Make sure every network login is over Kerberos, TLS or IKEv2: HTTPS-only admin pages on the firewall, switches and printers, and no FTP or Telnet logins.
Use MFA methods that are challenge- or time-based (Authenticator, TOTP, FIDO2) rather than reusable secrets, and prefer them over SMS.
Document the approved protocol list in the SSP and re-check it annually with a configuration review.

guidance.summary: When someone leaves or a device is retired, its username or identifier must not be handed to a different person or device for a defined period (many small shops simply choose 'never'). This keeps logs unambiguous: a log entry for 'jsmith' must always mean the same person.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's account management procedure states that usernames are never reused. Departed employees' accounts are disabled immediately, moved to a 'Disabled Users' OU for 90 days, and then deleted, but the username is recorded in an identifier register (a protected spreadsheet) so it is never re-issued. When a second J. Smith is hired, IT assigns jsmith2. The same rule applies to hostnames and service account names.
typical_evidence: Account management policy or procedure with the defined reuse period
Identifier register or AD export of disabled/retired accounts showing they are retained
Offboarding ticket showing the account was disabled rather than deleted or reassigned
Naming standard and an example of a suffixed username created to avoid a collision
common_gaps: No written period; a departed employee's account is renamed for the replacement
Shared or generic accounts passed from person to person
Accounts deleted immediately and the same username recreated for someone else
remediation_steps: Define the period in the account management policy (for example 'identifiers are never reused' or 'not for at least 2 years').
Change offboarding so the account is disabled, kept in a Disabled Users OU for at least the defined period, and the identifier is logged in a register before any deletion.
Adopt a naming standard with a numeric suffix rule to avoid collisions.
Apply the same rule to device names and service accounts.
During the annual account review, confirm no reserved identifier has been re-issued.

guidance.summary: Define how long an account may go unused (commonly 30 to 90 days) and disable it automatically or on a regular review once it passes that point. This catches forgotten contractor accounts, seasonal workers and service accounts nobody remembers.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Policy sets 45 days of inactivity for user accounts and 90 days for service accounts. The MSP runs a monthly scheduled PowerShell/Entra report of last sign-in and disables any user account past 45 days, attaching the list to a ticket. The admin approves exceptions in writing (for example an employee on medical leave) with an end date, and the local accounts on the controllers and firewall are checked by hand each quarter.
typical_evidence: Policy with the inactivity thresholds
Monthly inactive-account report and the ticket showing which accounts were disabled
Script schedule or Entra access review configuration
Exception list with approver and end date
common_gaps: No threshold defined; last-logon dates never checked
Service accounts and local accounts on controllers and the firewall not included
The report is produced but accounts stay enabled because nobody acts on it
remediation_steps: Set inactivity thresholds in policy (for example 45 days for users, 90 days for service accounts), covering domain, cloud and local accounts.
Automate a monthly last-logon report (AD lastLogonTimestamp, Entra sign-in activity) and the disable action; keep the output with each run.
Include local accounts on the server, controllers and firewall in a quarterly manual check.
Record exceptions with approver and end date, and re-enable accounts only through a ticket.

guidance.summary: Define minimum password rules (length and character mix) and a 'change of characters' rule (a new password must differ substantially from the old one), then enforce both technically whenever passwords are created or changed. Windows enforces length and complexity natively but not change of characters, so shops usually meet that objective with a banned-password or password-protection feature plus a long history, and state the rule in policy.
guidance.machine_shop_example: The shop's policy requires at least 14 characters with three of four character classes, no reuse of the previous 24 passwords, and a change-of-character rule that a new password may not simply add or change a few characters of the old one. The Default Domain Policy enforces length and complexity, Entra Password Protection (cloud plus the on-prem DC agent) rejects passwords containing the company name, 'machine', 'shop' or common substitutions, and the 24-password history blocks near-repeats. Local accounts on the controllers and firewall follow the same rule and are set manually by the admin.
typical_evidence: Password policy document stating the complexity and change-of-character requirements
Default Domain Policy or fine-grained password policy screenshot (minimum length, complexity enabled, history)
Entra Password Protection settings screenshot (custom banned list, on-premises enforcement mode)
Screenshot of a rejected weak or too-similar password change attempt
Record of how local accounts on controllers, the firewall and printers are held to the same rule
common_gaps: Windows default 7-character minimum still in place
Change-of-character requirement never defined
Controller, firewall and printer passwords not covered by any rule
MFA used as an excuse to leave weak passwords
remediation_steps: Write the rule: minimum 14 characters (or longer), complexity per your chosen benchmark, a new password must differ from the previous one by a defined amount, and passwords may not contain the username or banned words.
Enforce in AD with the Default Domain Policy or a fine-grained password policy: minimum length 14, complexity enabled, password history 24, minimum age 1 day.
Deploy Entra Password Protection (cloud and the on-premises agent on domain controllers) with a custom banned password list in enforce mode, which also blocks common substitutions of banned terms.
Apply equivalent settings to local accounts on the server, controllers, firewall and network devices where supported, and document manual enforcement where not.
Test by attempting a non-compliant password change and keep the screenshot as evidence.

guidance.summary: Specify how many previous passwords a user cannot reuse (Windows supports up to 24) and enforce it on every system that has its own passwords. Temporary passwords are exempt from lifetime rules.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Policy states 24 generations. The Default Domain Policy sets 'Enforce password history' to 24 with a 1-day minimum age, GCC High applies its tenant password history, and the ERP application (which has its own logins) is configured for 24 as well. The firewall admin and controller local accounts are covered procedurally: each password change is recorded in the vault, which shows the previous values are not reused.
typical_evidence: Password policy stating the number of generations
GPO or fine-grained password policy screenshot with Enforce password history = 24 and minimum password age set
GCC High tenant and ERP application password policy settings
Screenshot of a rejected reused password
common_gaps: History left at the default of 0 or a small number
Users cycle through minor variants (addressed together with 3.5.7 change-of-character)
Local accounts on devices with no history enforcement and no procedural record
remediation_steps: Set the number in policy (24 recommended).
Configure Enforce password history = 24 and a minimum password age of 1 day in AD to stop rapid cycling back to an old password.
Confirm the GCC High tenant and any application with its own passwords (ERP, controller software) enforce history or are covered procedurally with vault records.
Test a reuse attempt and keep the screenshot.

guidance.summary: When IT gives a new hire, or a user with a reset, a temporary password, the system must force them to set their own permanent password at first logon. This applies to AD, GCC High, the VPN, the ERP and any local account you hand out, including temporary vendor accounts.
guidance.machine_shop_example: New user accounts are created with 'User must change password at next logon' checked in AD, and GCC High onboarding uses a Temporary Access Pass that expires after first use and forces MFA registration and a permanent password. The MSP help desk procedure requires the same flag on every password reset. Temporary local admin passwords issued to a vendor are one-time because LAPS rotates the password automatically after the visit.
typical_evidence: Account provisioning and reset procedure requiring a unique temporary password and the change-at-next-logon flag
Screenshot of AD user properties with 'User must change password at next logon' set; Entra force-change or Temporary Access Pass policy
Sample onboarding and reset tickets showing the step
Screenshot of the first-logon prompt forcing a change
common_gaps: The help desk hands out a standard 'Welcome123!' that users keep
The flag is set on new accounts but not on password resets
Shared temporary passwords for controllers or vendors that are never changed afterwards
remediation_steps: Update the provisioning and reset procedures: every temporary password is unique, delivered out of band, and flagged for change at next logon.
Configure 'User must change password at next logon' in AD and force password change in Entra on creation and reset; use Temporary Access Pass for MFA-first onboarding in GCC High.
Train the MSP help desk on the procedure and audit a sample of reset tickets each quarter.
Use LAPS so any temporary local administrator password rotates automatically after use.

guidance.summary: Passwords must be stored only as salted one-way hashes and sent over the network only inside encrypted channels. In practice: no passwords in plain-text files, spreadsheets, scripts or sticky notes; no logins over HTTP, FTP or Telnet; reversible encryption disabled in AD; and a proper password manager for IT and MSP credentials.
guidance.machine_shop_example: AD stores password hashes with reversible encryption disabled and LM hash storage off, Entra stores hashes, and the shop uses a password manager with MFA for the admin and MSP shared credentials instead of the old spreadsheet, which was deleted after migration. All logins run over Kerberos, TLS (HTTPS to GCC High, the ERP web portal with a valid certificate) or the IKEv2 VPN; the firewall, switch and printer admin pages are HTTPS-only with HTTP disabled. The backup job and the CNC program-transfer script use a group managed service account and SFTP rather than embedded passwords.
typical_evidence: GPO export showing 'Store passwords using reversible encryption' disabled and 'Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change' enabled
Password manager or vault in use (screenshot, access list) and policy prohibiting plain-text password storage
Configuration showing HTTPS-only management on the firewall, switches and printers with FTP/Telnet/HTTP disabled
Vulnerability scan or configuration review showing no cleartext authentication protocols in use
Review record of scripts and scheduled tasks confirming no embedded credentials
common_gaps: An IT password spreadsheet or Word document on the file server
Passwords embedded in backup or CNC transfer scripts
Printers, scanners or controllers using HTTP or FTP logins
Reversible encryption enabled for an old application
remediation_steps: Set by GPO: reversible encryption disabled and LM hash storage disabled; verify no accounts have the 'store password using reversible encryption' flag.
Move all IT and MSP credentials into a password manager protected by MFA; delete the spreadsheet or document after migration and record that it was destroyed.
Replace cleartext logins: HTTPS with valid certificates for the firewall, switches, printers and ERP; disable HTTP, FTP and Telnet; use SFTP for any controller file transfer that requires a login.
Find and remove embedded credentials in scripts and scheduled tasks; use group managed service accounts or vault retrieval instead.
Add 'no plain-text passwords' to policy and check quarterly with a search of the file server and mailboxes for password files.

guidance.summary: When someone types a password, the screen must not display it (dots or asterisks instead), on every login interface in scope: Windows, the CNC controller software, the ERP, web admin pages, the VPN client and the firewall. A brief 'show last character' on small screens is acceptable; a login that echoes the whole password is not.
guidance.machine_shop_example: Windows, GCC High, the VPN client and the ERP login all mask passwords by default. The admin checked the CNC controller software and the ERP web portal, confirmed masking, and filed a screenshot of each in the evidence folder. The policy notes that users must not use 'show password' where others can see the screen, and the two shop-floor monitors were turned away from the walkway.
typical_evidence: Screenshots of each login screen in scope (Windows, controller software, ERP, VPN, firewall/switch admin pages) showing masked input
Policy statement covering obscured authentication feedback and shoulder surfing
Checklist item for verifying masking when a new application or device is introduced
common_gaps: A custom or legacy shop-floor application that echoes the password
Assumed but never verified for the controllers and device admin pages
Passwords displayed in plain text during shared remote-support sessions
remediation_steps: Inventory every login interface in scope (OS, controller software, ERP, web admin pages, VPN, password manager).
Verify each one masks input, capture a screenshot, and fix or replace any that do not (vendor setting or upgrade).
Add the requirement to the authentication policy and to the checklist for onboarding new applications and devices.
Instruct the MSP not to display passwords in shared or recorded sessions.
